narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the admissions model predicted a 57.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In plain terms, the model viewed failure as more likely than success, and that risk was too high for admission.

The most influential factor in that decision was your first-year class standing. You ranked in the lowest decile among your classmates in Year 1, while students who were admitted typically sat around the sixth decile. That early academic rank was the single strongest signal pushing the prediction toward bar exam failure, and it weighed heavily against you.

Your undergraduate GPA, surprisingly, worked in your favor. At 3.40, you were above the average of 3.23 for accepted applicants, making it the second most influential factor overall. It pulled the prediction in the direction of passing, which suggests you are capable of strong academic work. However, this positive signal was not enough to outweigh your concerning law school performance.

The third most important factor was your third-year class standing. You finished in the second-lowest decile, compared to an average around the sixth decile for admitted students. This reinforced the pattern already seen in your first-year rank: across your law school career, you tended to fall near the bottom of your class, which the model linked strongly to bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 32 is also well below the average of 37, and your family income background differs from most admitted students, but these played a smaller role than your academic ranks.

What should you do next? Focus on demonstrated improvement. Consider retaking the LSAT, enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program to strengthen your academic record, and building evidence of recent academic success. If you can show sustained upward performance in a rigorous setting, you can counter the negative signal from your law school class standings when you reapply.
